translation: This means: "Homage" signifies bowing with devotion. To whom does one bow? She is Tārā (sgrol ma) because she delivers sentient beings from saṃsāra. She is the Swift One (mgyur ma) because her enlightened activity is swifter than that of other Victors. She is the Heroic Lady (dpal mo) because she vanquishes the hosts of māras without remainder. Her wisdom eyes are like a momentary flash of lightning, as she perceives all knowable objects in a single instant. The protector and refuge of the three worlds—the subterranean world of the nāgas, the terrestrial world of humans, and the celestial world of the gods—is the Noble Avalokiteśvara, and she is the one who possesses the history of having arisen from the opening stamens of a lotus flower that was born from the tears resting upon the maṇḍala of his face; thus, one bows to her. As the Great Translator Namzang emended the third line to read "the lotus of the face of the Lord of the Three Worlds," it is easier to understand, and so it is explained accordingly.

translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To her who possesses a face that is supremely white and beautiful, like a hundred full autumn moons—the season free from dust, clouds, and sheep-wool-like mists—gathered and piled together, the moon being at its full, having completed its waxing and not yet having begun to wane. translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To her whose body color is beautiful like the gold of the Jambu river and has a slightly blue appearance; whose left hand is perfectly adorned with the thumb and ring finger holding a water-born lotus—that is, an utpala—with its petals blossomed near her ear as a sign; and who has arisen from having made the six perfections—generosity, diligence, the ethical discipline of difficult-to-guard austerities, the wisdom that pacifies the darkness of ignorance, patience, and meditative concentration—the very sphere of her manifest activity.

heading: ལྔ་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ལྷ་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཀུར་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
source: ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། ཤར་གྱི་ཕྱོགས་སྐྱོང་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་དང༌། ཤར་ལྷོའི་མེ་ལྷ་དང༌། སྟེང་གི་ཚངས་པ་དང་། ནུབ་བྱུང་གི་རླུང་ལྷ་དང༌། དེ་དག་གིས་མཚོན་པའི་གཤིན་རྗེ་དང་ཀླུ་སོགས་སྡེ་རིས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་དབང་ཕྱུག་སྟེ་གཙོ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གུས་པས་མཆོད་པའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་མ། དབང་ལྡན་གྱི་འཁོར་འབྱུང་པོ་རྣམས་དང༌། སྲིན་པོའི་འཁོར་རོ་ལངས་རྣམས་དང༌། བརྒྱ་བྱིན་གྱི་འཁོར་དྲི་ཟ་རྣམས་དང༌། ལུས་ངན་གྱི་འཁོར་གནོད་སྦྱིན་སོགས་འཁོར་གྱི་ཚོགས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་སྐུ་མདུན་དུ་བཏུད་ནས་གུས་པས་བསྟོད་པའི་ཡུལ་དུ་གྱུར་མ་དེ་ལའོ། །
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To her who is the object of respectful worship by the great ones—the lords of various classes of beings—such as the guardian of the eastern direction, Indra; the fire god of the southeast; Brahmā of the zenith; the wind god of the northwest; and, represented by these, Yama, the Nāgas, and others. She is the one who has become the object of praise, offered with reverence by the hosts of her retinue, who bow before her: the Bhūtas in the retinue of Īśvara, the Vetālas in the retinue of the Rākṣasas, the Gandharvas in the retinue of Indra, and the Yakṣas in the retinue of the "ugly-bodied" ones.

heading: དྲུག་པ་ཕ་རོལ་འཇོམས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To her who, merely by the sound of the vidyā-mantras "Traṭ" (meaning to tear apart, or conquer) and "Phaṭ" (meaning to burst) from her mouth, utterly destroys in an instant all the power of the magical wheels created by the evil thoughts and actions of hostile sorcerers. With her right leg drawn in and left extended—symbolizing emptiness and compassion—she tramples underfoot the sorcerers, the rbad-’dre spirits, and the like. From her body, a fire of primordial wisdom blazes and swirls, and by its intense burning, she consumes them completely, leaving not even ash behind. Although her posture is that of a peaceful deity, her dwelling in the midst of a blazing fire represents a slightly wrathful aspect.

heading: དང་པོ་བདུད་དང་སྒྲིབ་གཉིས་སྦྱོང་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the one who is Ture (the Swift One) and so forth, by way of the sound of her speech, and the Great Fearful One, by way of the manifestation of her extremely wrathful body. She who utterly destroys the champions of Mara—the champions among the demons who are difficult to tame—is the one who destroys the four Maras of mental affliction. By means of her lotus face—beautiful like a blossoming lotus—which she makes to have a frowning expression, she is the one who slays all external enemies as well, without leaving any remainder. Here, if one interprets the enemies of liberation as the afflictive obscurations and the enemies of omniscience as the cognitive obscurations, it accords with the summary meaning.

Blazing like the fire at the end of an eon;
With right leg extended and left bent, she is surrounded by joy,

To the one who dwells in the midst of a turbulent garland of blazing fire of primordial wisdom, which is like the fire at the time of the destruction of the world at the end of an eon. འབར་བའི་འཕྲེང་བའི་དབུས་ན་གནས་མ། །

དགྲ་ཡི་དཔུང་ནི་རྣམ་པར་འཇོམས་མ། །
[2-38] translation already produced for this document:
Homage to her who dwells within a garland of fire
Blazing like the fire at the end of an eon;
With right leg extended and left bent, she is surrounded by joy,
And she completely destroys the armies of enemies.

[2-39] source:
ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། བསྐལ་པ་ཐ་མའི་མེས་འཇིག་གི་དུས་ཀྱི་མེ་ལྟར་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མེ་དཔུང་འབར་བའི་འཕྲེང་བ་འཁྲུག་པའི་དབུས་ན་གནས་མ། དེ་ཡང་ཞབས་གཡས་བརྐྱངས་ཤིང་གཡོན་བསྐུམས་པའི་སྟབས་ཀྱིས་བཞུགས་ནས། སྒོ་ཀུན་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁོར་ལོ་བསྐོར་བ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གདུལ་བྱའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཕྱི་ནང་གི་དགྲ་ཡི་དཔུང་ཚོགས་རྣམ་པར་འཇོམས་པར་མཛད་མ་དེ་ལའོ། །
[2-39] translation already produced for this document:
This means: Homage. To whom? To the one who dwells in the midst of a turbulent garland of blazing fire of primordial wisdom, which is like the fire at the time of the destruction of the world at the end of an eon. Furthermore, she abides in a posture with her right leg extended and her left leg bent, and she completely destroys the hosts of outer and inner enemies in the continuums of those to be tamed who delight in the turning of the wheel of Dharma from every perspective.

heading: བདུན་པ་ཧཱུཾ་ཡིག་ལས་འོད་ཟེར་འཕྲོ་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation:
Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth
With the palms of her hands and tramples it with her feet;
With a wrathful frown and the syllable Hūṃ,
She shatters the seven levels.

source: ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། རི་རབ་གླིང་དང་བཅས་པའི་ས་གཞི་ཆེན་པོའི་ངོས་ལ། སྡིགས་མཛུབ་དང་བཅས་པའི་ཕྱག་གི་མཐིལ་གྱིས་དྲག་ཏུ་བསྣུན་ཅིང་ཞབས་ཀྱི་མཐིལ་གྱིས་བརྡུང་བར་མཛད་མ། དེ་ཡང་ཞལ་ཁྲོ་གཉེར་བསྡུས་པ་སོགས་ཤིན་ཏུ་དྲག་མོའི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་དུ་མཛད་པའི་ཕྱག་ཞབས་ཀྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་ཡི་གེ་ཧཾ་སྔོན་པོ་རེ་རེ་གནས་པ་ལས་རྡོ་རྗེའི་མེ་ཆར་སྤྲོས་པས། གཞི་དང༌། ལྷག་པའི་གཞི་དང༌། གཞི་མེད་པ་དང་། གཞི་ཉིད་དང༌། བཅུད་ཀྱི་གཞི་དང༌། །གཞི་བཟང་པོ་དང༌། དག་པའི་གཞི་སྟེ། ས་འོག་རིམ་པ་བདུན་པོ་ན་གནས་པའི་ཀླུ་དང་ལྷ་མིན་དང་གཤིན་རྗེ་སོགས་གདུག་པ་ཅན་རྣམས་ནི་འགེམས་པ་སྟེ་འཇོམས་པར་མཛད་མ་དེ་ལའོ། །
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the one who strikes the surface of the great earth, including Mount Meru and the continents, with the palms of her hands—which are accompanied by the threatening mudrā—and tramples it with the soles of her feet. Furthermore, she assumes a highly wrathful appearance, such as by contracting her face into a frown, and from the blue syllable Hūṃ residing in the center of each of her palms and soles, she emanates a rain of vajra fire. Thereby, she shatters—that is, she destroys—the malevolent beings such as the Nāgas, Asuras, and Yamas who dwell in the seven levels beneath the earth, namely: the basis, the superior basis, the baseless, the basis itself, the basis of essence, the good basis, and the pure basis.

heading: གཉིས་པ་ཆོས་སྐུའི་རྣམ་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
source: ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། འབྲས་བུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མེད་པས་བདེ་མ། །རྒྱུ་མི་དགེ་བ་མི་གསོག་པས་དགེ་མ། སྤང་བྱ་ཉོན་མོངས་མེད་པས་ཞི་མ། སྒྲིབ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཞི་བ་མཆོག་གི་དབྱིངས་ལ་རྟག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་པས་དེའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཉིད་དུ་གྱུར་པ། དེའི་མཐུས་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པའི་རིག་སྔགས། ཏཱ་རེ་ཏུཏྟཱ་རེ་ཏུ་རེ། ཞེས་པ་མཇུག་ཏུ་སྭཱ་ཧཱ་དང༌། འགོར་ཨོཾ་དང་ཡང་དག་པར་ལྡན་པར་བྱས་པའི་ཡི་གེ་བཅུ་པ་ཉིད་ཚེས་བཞིན་དུ་བཟླས་པས་ཟློས་པ་པོའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་མཚམས་མེད་ལྔ་དང་ཆོས་སྤོང་སོགས་སྡིག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་དང༌། དེའི་རྒྱུ་ཆགས་སྡང་སོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་དང༌། འབྲས་བུ་ཚ་གྲང་སོགས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ལྷག་མེད་དུ་འཇོམས་པར་མཛད་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་མ་དེ་ལའོ། །
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the one who is "Blissful" because she is free from the result of suffering; "Virtuous" because she does not accumulate the cause of non-virtue; and "Peaceful" because she is free from the afflictions to be abandoned. Because she constantly rests in equipoise within the supreme expanse of peace that has passed beyond the sorrow of the two obscurations, she has become one whose very sphere of experience is that. By the power of that, the mantra she has spoken—Tāre Tuttāre Ture—when practiced like the waxing moon, having been made perfectly endowed with Svāhā at the end and Oṃ at the beginning, and consisting of ten syllables, utterly destroys without remainder the great negativities of the practitioner’s continuum, such as the five inexpiable sins and the abandonment of the Dharma; their causes, the great afflictions such as attachment and aversion; and their results, the great sufferings such as heat and cold. To that essence of a mother, I pay homage.

heading: དང་པོ་ཞི་ཁྲོའི་སྔགས་ཀྱི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who utterly shatters and destroys the bodies of the outer and inner enemies in the mental continuums of those to be tamed who take great delight in the turning of the Dharma wheel in every way. Regarding that, for the peaceful aspect, at the heart is the Tāṃ syllable, followed by the ten-syllable speech, that is, the mantra: OṂ TĀRE TUTTĀRE TURE SVĀHĀ. Because it is this, it is by way of arranging that. For the wrathful aspect, at the heart is the awareness, that is, the awareness mantra: OṂ NAMO TĀRE NAMO HARE HŪṂ HARE SVĀHĀ. By way of the Hūṃ syllable placed in the center of that which is surrounded by this, light rays and so forth are emanated, and thus it is to that Tārā herself who destroys enemies, obstructers, and so forth.

Because it is this, it is by way of arranging that. For the wrathful aspect, at the heart is the awareness, that is, the awareness mantra: OṂ NAMO TĀRE NAMO HARE HŪṂ HARE SVĀHĀ. By way of the Hūṃ syllable placed in the center of that which is surrounded by this, light rays and so forth are emanated, and thus it is to that Tārā herself who destroys enemies, obstructers, and so forth.

heading: གཉིས་པ་ཁྲོ་མོས་ས་གསུམ་གཡོ་བའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who stamps Her two feet—the Ture, meaning the Swift One—violently. What is that Swift One like? She is the embodiment of the wrathful one born from the seed-syllable in the form of the syllable Hāṃ. What does She do by stamping Her feet? She causes the king of mountains, Mount Meru, the mountain Mandara, the black mountain Vindhya, and so forth—in short, the three worlds of the subterranean, the terrestrial, and the celestial, along with their inhabitants—to tremble. Therefore, it is to that One who is the embodiment of such power and strength.

This means: Homage. To whom? Regarding that, for the peaceful aspect, at the heart is the Tāṃ syllable, followed by the ten-syllable speech, that is, the mantra: OṂ TĀRE TUTTĀRE TURE SVĀHĀ. Because it is this, it is by way of arranging that. For the wrathful aspect, at the heart is the awareness, that is, the awareness mantra: OṂ NAMO TĀRE NAMO HARE HŪṂ HARE SVĀHĀ. This means: Homage. To whom? It is to that One.

heading: ལྔ་པ་རིམས་ནད་སེལ་བའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation:
Homage to the One whose two eyes,
Like the full sun and moon, radiate brilliant light;
By uttering the two *hara*s and *tuttāra*,
She clears away the most violent infectious diseases.

heading: ལྔ་པ་རིམས་ནད་སེལ་བའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who possesses light that is brilliantly radiant and cool from Her two wrathful eyes, which are like the full sun, and Her two peaceful eyes, which are like the full moon. By reciting the wrathful mantra, indicated by the two *hara*s (meaning "to snatch away"), which is *oṃ namaḥ tāre namo hare hūṃ hare svāhā*, and the peaceful mantra, indicated by *tuttāra*, which is *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*, She clears away even all the most violent—that is, difficult to cure—infectious diseases without exception. It is to that One.

source: ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། སྒྲུབ་པ་པོ་ལྷ་མོའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་གནས་པའི་སྤྱི་པོར་སྐུའི་དེ་ཉིད་ཨོཾ། མགྲིན་པར་གསུང་གི་དེ་ཉིད་ཨཱཿ སྙིང་གར་ཐུགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཉིད་ཧཱུཾ་སྟེ་དེ་ཉིད་གསུམ་པོ་དེ་རྣམས་གནས་གསུམ་དུ་བཀོད་ནས་བསྒོམ་པས་སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཉེར་འཚེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལྷག་མེད་དུ་ཞི་བའི་མཐུ་ནུས་དང་ཡང་དག་པར་ལྡན་མ། ནམ་གྲུའི་གདོན་ལ་སོགས་པ་གདོན་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་དང༌། རོ་ལངས་ཀྱི་ལས་རྦོད་གཏོང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངན་སྔགས་དང༌། མདངས་འཕྲོག་པའི་གནོད་སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གནོད་པའི་ཚོགས་རྣམས། མྱུར་དུ་འཇོམས་པའི་མཆོག་དང་རབ་ཀྱི་བདག་ཉིད་མ་དེ་ལ་སྟེ། རྗེ་བཙུན་འགྲོ་བའི་མགོན་པོས། ཚིག་རྐང་བཞི་པར། མྱུར་དུ་འཇོམས་པའི་མཆོག་རབ་ཉིད་མ། །ཞེས་འགྱུར་བཅོས་མཛད་པ་ལྟར་བཤད་དེ། ཏུ་རེ་ཞེས་པ་མྱུར་མའམ། སྐབས་ཐོབ་ཀྱིས་མྱུར་དུ་ལའང་འཇུག་པས་སོ། །
translation: This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who is perfectly endowed with the power and ability to pacify, without remainder, all obstacles of the three doors, by meditating upon the arrangement of the three suchnesses at the three places—the suchness of body, *oṃ*, at the crown; the suchness of speech, *āḥ*, at the throat; and the suchness of mind, *hūṃ*, at the heart—of the practitioner who abides in the yoga of the Goddess. She is the supreme mistress who swiftly destroys the hosts of harmful beings, such as the eighteen types of spirits including the *nam-gru* spirits, the evil mantras such as the *ro-langs* (zombie) rituals of casting spells, and the *yakṣas* who steal one's vitality. This is explained according to the emendation made by the Lord, the Protector of Beings, in the fourth line: "She is the supreme *Ture* who destroys," because *ture* means "the swift one," or, depending on the context, it also functions as "the swift [act of] destroying."

Work: དངུལ་ཆུ་དྷརྨ་བྷ་དྲའི་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཉེར་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟོད་པའི་རྣམ་བཤད། (author: Ngulchu Dharmabhadra). A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated one at a time, in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-61] source:
དྲུག་པ་གདོན་དང་རོ་ལངས་འཇོམས་པའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པ་ནི།
[2-61] translation already produced for this document:
The sixth is the praise by way of the enlightened activity of subduing spirits and zombies:

[2-62] source:
ཕྱག་འཚལ་དེ་ཉིད་གསུམ་རྣམས་བཀོད་པས། །
ཞི་བའི་མཐུ་དང་ཡང་དག་ལྡན་མ། །
གདོན་དང་རོ་ལངས་གནོད་སྦྱིན་ཚོགས་རྣམས། །
འཇོམས་པ་ཏུ་རེ་རབ་མཆོག་ཉིད་མ། །
[2-62] translation already produced for this document:
Homage to the One who, by arranging the three suchnesses,
Is perfectly endowed with the power of pacification;
She is the supreme *Ture* who destroys
The hosts of spirits, zombies, and *yakṣas*.

[2-63] source:
ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གང་ལ་ན། སྒྲུབ་པ་པོ་ལྷ་མོའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་གནས་པའི་སྤྱི་པོར་སྐུའི་དེ་ཉིད་ཨོཾ། མགྲིན་པར་གསུང་གི་དེ་ཉིད་ཨཱཿ སྙིང་གར་ཐུགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཉིད་ཧཱུཾ་སྟེ་དེ་ཉིད་གསུམ་པོ་དེ་རྣམས་གནས་གསུམ་དུ་བཀོད་ནས་བསྒོམ་པས་སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཉེར་འཚེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལྷག་མེད་དུ་ཞི་བའི་མཐུ་ནུས་དང་ཡང་དག་པར་ལྡན་མ། ནམ་གྲུའི་གདོན་ལ་སོགས་པ་གདོན་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་དང༌། རོ་ལངས་ཀྱི་ལས་རྦོད་གཏོང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངན་སྔགས་དང༌། མདངས་འཕྲོག་པའི་གནོད་སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གནོད་པའི་ཚོགས་རྣམས། མྱུར་དུ་འཇོམས་པའི་མཆོག་དང་རབ་ཀྱི་བདག་ཉིད་མ་དེ་ལ་སྟེ། རྗེ་བཙུན་འགྲོ་བའི་མགོན་པོས། ཚིག་རྐང་བཞི་པར། མྱུར་དུ་འཇོམས་པའི་མཆོག་རབ་ཉིད་མ། །ཞེས་འགྱུར་བཅོས་མཛད་པ་ལྟར་བཤད་དེ། ཏུ་རེ་ཞེས་པ་མྱུར་མའམ། སྐབས་ཐོབ་ཀྱིས་མྱུར་དུ་ལའང་འཇུག་པས་སོ། །
[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who is perfectly endowed with the power and ability to pacify, without remainder, all obstacles of the three doors, by meditating upon the arrangement of the three suchnesses at the three places—the suchness of body, *oṃ*, at the crown; the suchness of speech, *āḥ*, at the throat; and the suchness of mind, *hūṃ*, at the heart—of the practitioner who abides in the yoga of the Goddess. She is the supreme mistress who swiftly destroys the hosts of harmful beings, such as the eighteen types of spirits including the *nam-gru* spirits, the evil mantras such as the *ro-langs* (zombie) rituals of casting spells, and the *yakṣas* who steal one's vitality. This is explained according to the emendation made by the Lord, the Protector of Beings, in the fourth line: "She is the supreme *Ture* who destroys," because *ture* means "the swift one," or, depending on the context, it also functions as "the swift [act of] destroying."

heading: དང་པོ་བསམ་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation:
This praise with the root mantra,
And these twenty-one homages,
By any intelligent person
Endowed with genuine devotion to the Goddess,
Who recites them clearly—

heading: དང་པོ་བསམ་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: This means: Because it is combined with the two root mantras of the peaceful and wrathful [Tārās], this praise of the twenty-one Tārās contains twenty-one verses, and the text itself, which contains twenty-one "homages," should be recited with great devotion and the thought that the benefits mentioned below will arise for any person who possesses supreme intelligence capable of distinguishing good from bad, who is endowed with genuine devotion and remembrance of the kindness of the Goddess Tārā, and who recites it with firm, supreme faith that remembers her qualities according to the meaning of the words.

This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who is perfectly endowed with the power and ability to pacify, without remainder, all obstacles of the three doors, by meditating upon the arrangement of the three suchnesses at the three places—the suchness of body, *oṃ*, at the crown; the suchness of speech, *āḥ*, at the throat; and the suchness of mind, *hūṃ*, at the heart—of the practitioner who abides in the yoga of the Goddess. She is the supreme mistress who swiftly destroys the hosts of harmful beings, such as the eighteen types of spirits including the *nam-gru* spirits, the evil mantras such as the *ro-langs* (zombie) rituals of casting spells, and the *yakṣas* who steal one's vitality. This is explained according to the emendation made by the Lord, the Protector of Beings, in the fourth line: "She is the supreme *Ture* who destroys," because *ture* means "the swift one," or, depending on the context, it also functions as "the swift [act of] destroying."

Having arisen at dusk and at dawn,
Through mindfulness, all fearlessness is fully bestowed;
All misdeeds are thoroughly pacified,
And all lower realms are utterly destroyed.

heading: གཉིས་པ་དུས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: This means: If one prays because of fear of illness, malevolent spirits, enemies, thieves, and so forth in this life, one should recite the praise at dusk while primarily recollecting the wrathful form and so forth. If one prays because of fear of the suffering of lower realms in the future, one should recite the praise at dawn, having arisen from bed, while primarily recollecting the peaceful form and so forth. Because this destroys the eight great internal and external fears, it "fully bestows all fearlessness," and because it thoroughly pacifies all misdeeds, such as the ten non-virtues which are the causes of lower realms, it has the benefit of "utterly destroying" all lower realms, such as the hells, which are the results. This shows that one must act in accordance with the specific time.

Will swiftly bestow empowerment,
They will attain even greater excellence than this,
And proceed to that ultimate state of Buddhahood.

heading: ཡོན་ཏན་འཐོབ་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།
translation: This means: The seventy million Victorious Ones—the emanated forms who reside together with the Bhagavatī herself—will swiftly, that is, in this very life, bestow empowerment through a stream of light rays or nectar. By the power of that, one will attain, in the temporary sense, a state of excellence in terms of life, body, enjoyments, and retinue that is greater and more supreme than one's current situation. In the ultimate sense, one will swiftly traverse the path and proceed to that state of Buddhahood. This is the meaning; some translations of the fourth line explain it as "proceed to the ultimate state of Buddhahood."

This means: If one prays because of fear of illness, malevolent spirits, enemies, thieves, and so forth in this life, one should recite the praise at dusk while primarily recollecting the wrathful form and so forth. If one prays because of fear of the suffering of lower realms in the future, one should recite the praise at dawn, having arisen from bed, while primarily recollecting the peaceful form and so forth. Because this destroys the eight great internal and external fears, it "fully bestows all fearlessness," and because it thoroughly pacifies all misdeeds, such as the ten non-virtues which are the causes of lower realms, it has the benefit of "utterly destroying" all lower realms, such as the hells, which are the results. This shows that one must act in accordance with the specific time.

translation: This means: The poisons such as attachment, which are afflictions that obstruct the attainment of the temporary and ultimate benefits and cause great suffering, are "fierce" because they rob one of the life of high status and definite goodness, and they are "great" because they generate the suffering of cyclic existence and the lower realms. Regarding these, as well as poisons that are "stationary," such as aconite found in the inanimate world, or "moving," such as snake venom found in sentient beings—even if one has eaten, drunk, or touched them, by merely remembering the Goddess’s form and reciting the praise, one will attain complete purification.

Seventy million Victorious Ones
Will swiftly bestow empowerment,
They will attain even greater excellence than this,
And proceed to that ultimate state of Buddhahood.

[3-9] translation already produced for this document:
This means: The seventy million Victorious Ones—the emanated forms who reside together with the Bhagavatī herself—will swiftly, that is, in this very life, bestow empowerment through a stream of light rays or nectar. By the power of that, one will attain, in the temporary sense, a state of excellence in terms of life, body, enjoyments, and retinue that is greater and more supreme than one's current situation. In the ultimate sense, one will swiftly traverse the path and proceed to that state of Buddhahood. This is the meaning; some translations of the fourth line explain it as "proceed to the ultimate state of Buddhahood."

Whether stationary or moving,
Even if they have been eaten or drunk,

ཅེས་པ་སྟེ། གནས་སྐབས་དང་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་བར་དུ་གཅོད་ཅིང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཚབས་ཆེན་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་དུག་ཆགས་སོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་ནི། མངོན་མཐོ་དང་ངེས་ལེགས་ཀྱི་སྲོག་འཕྲོག་པས་ན་དྲག་པོ་དང་། འཁོར་བ་དང་ངན་སོང་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བསྐྱེད་པས་ན་ཆེན་པོ་ཡིན་པས་དེ་དང་། བཙན་དུག་སོགས་བརྟན་པར་གནས་པ་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་ཡོད་པའམ། གཞན་ཡང་སྦྲུལ་དུག་སོགས་གཡོ་ཞིང་འཕྲོས་བཅུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་དུག་རྣམས་ཁར་ཟོས་པ་དང་ནི་འཐུངས་པ་དང་རེག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་། ལྷ་མོའི་སྐུ་སོགས་དྲན་ནས་བསྟོད་པ་བརྗོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་རབ་ཏུ་སེལ་བ་ཉིད་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-12] translation already produced for this document:
This means: The poisons such as attachment, which are afflictions that obstruct the attainment of the temporary and ultimate benefits and cause great suffering, are "fierce" because they rob one of the life of high status and definite goodness, and they are "great" because they generate the suffering of cyclic existence and the lower realms. Regarding these, as well as poisons that are "stationary," such as aconite found in the inanimate world, or "moving," such as snake venom found in sentient beings—even if one has eaten, drunk, or touched them, by merely remembering the Goddess’s form and reciting the praise, one will attain complete purification.

heading: གཉིས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལྡོག་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།
translation:
The masses of suffering of those tormented
By demons, epidemics, and poisons, are utterly cast off.

translation: This commentary on the Praise to the Twenty-One Tārās, entitled A Bouquet of Utpala Flowers that Captures the Mind, is based upon the commentary of Paṇchen Gendun Drub. I have gathered the best points from the commentaries of Jetsun Drakpa Gyaltsen, the Omniscient Gendun Gyatso, and Jetsun Tāranātha. Having also slightly harmonized it with the traditions of the glorious sole deity Dīpaṃkara and Paṇchen Nyima Bepa, it was composed by the Śākya monk Dharmabhadra in the mountain retreat of Ngulchu, on an auspicious day during the waxing moon of the month of Dabo in the year of the Mouse. May it be of benefit to the teachings and beings, even after I have passed. Maṅgalam.

heading: དང་པོ་བསམ་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation:
This praise with the root mantra,
And these twenty-one homages,
By any intelligent person endowed with genuine devotion to the Goddess,
Who recites them clearly,

[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
This means: Homage. To whom? To the One who is perfectly endowed with the power and ability to pacify, without remainder, all obstacles of the three doors, by meditating upon the arrangement of the three suchnesses at the three places—the suchness of body, *oṃ*, at the crown; the suchness of speech, *āḥ*, at the throat; and the suchness of mind, *hūṃ*, at the heart—of the practitioner who abides in the yoga of the Goddess. She is the supreme mistress who swiftly destroys the hosts of harmful beings, such as the eighteen types of spirits including the *nam-gru* spirits, the evil mantras such as the *ro-langs* (zombie) rituals of casting spells, and the *yakṣas* who steal one's vitality. This is explained according to the emendation made by the Lord, the Protector of Beings, in the fourth line: "She is the supreme *Ture* who destroys," because *ture* means "the swift one," or, depending on the context, it also functions as "the swift [act of] destroying."
